newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Somali faction leaders meet in Ethiopia.
newsitem.headline: Somali faction leaders meet in Ethiopia.

text.p: Somali faction leaders are meeting in Ethiopia in efforts to try to organise a national reconciliation conference for their broken Horn of Africa country, Ethiopian officials said on Wednesday.
A foreign ministry official said the talks involving some 26 faction leaders were taking place at Soder, some 100 kms (60 miles) east of the capital Addis Ababa.

Most prominent at the meeting is north Mogadishu faction leader and self-styled president, Ali Mahdi Mohamed. His chief rival, a south Mogadishu faction leader who is also a claimant to the presidency, Hussein Aideed, is boycotting the meeting.
Hussein Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine, took over as the main faction chief in war-shattered south Mogadishu when his 62-year-old father Mohamed Farah Aideed died on August 1.
His authority is contested by other Somali clans but analysts say a reconciliation conference without the participation of Aideed's militarily powerful Habr Gedir clan is useless.

Somalia has been without central authority since 1991 when rebels overthrew late president Mohamed Siad Barre. But they soon turned their guns on each other in murderous battles that laid waste to Somalia.
State-run Ethiopia News Agency (ENA) said the Somali leaders had established a National Coordinating Council tasked with preparing a conference to reconcile the warring factions.
The Coordinating Council will work out dates and a venue for the conference but no details have been released yet.
In remarks carried by ENA, Foreign Minister Seyoum Mesfin called on the Somalis to work towards peace in their country and help stabilise the Horn of Africa.

"Our region as a whole can never achieve durable peace and security without the establishment of a legitimate central authority in Somalia and without national reconciliation in that sisterly country," the minister said.

Countless efforts by African countries and the international community to reconcile Somalis and help create a new central administration have failed in the past mainly because of unending rivarly between Ali Mahdi and Aideed's factions.
